tagline: From downtown park squares to wooded neighborhoods along Baltimore’s dividing street
intro: Charles Street carries an urban drive from Baltimore’s Inner Harbor area through downtown, monument squares and wooded residential neighborhoods toward Lutherville. Maryland’s tourism office presents this 12-mile National Scenic Byway as a route through the city’s cultural, residential and commercial life. Its itinerary allows an hour to drive and one or two days to explore.

The street began in Baltimore’s 1730 plan as Forest Street, with its southern end at present-day Lombard Street. It was called Charles Street by at least 1761. The county section was paved in stages, completed in 1928 and marked as Maryland Route 139 by 1933. Within the city, Charles remains the boundary for East and West street names and address numbering. Widening and relocation in the county during the 1950s produced sections of four-lane divided highway.

Heading north from South Baltimore, pass the Inner Harbor area and downtown churches before Charles Street divides beside Mount Vernon’s park squares. Continue through Charles Village to Johns Hopkins University’s Homewood campus, then through the wooded northern neighborhoods. Beyond the city line, the road curves through a forested section and reaches Lutherville near the Baltimore Beltway. On their paired section, Charles Street carries northbound MD 139 and St. Paul Street its southbound counterpart.

moments.title: Washington Monument, Mount Vernon Place
moments.text: Robert Mills’s Washington Monument shows the general surrendering command of the Continental Army. Mills later designed the Washington monument on the National Mall. Baltimore’s cornerstone was laid in 1815 on land donated by John Eager Howard, and the masonry was completed in 1829. The marble came from three quarries in Baltimore County. Bronze inscriptions added in the 1830s record eight events in Washington’s life. The column rises from a square gallery base, crowned by the standing figure. Mills also designed the cast-iron fence at the base, added in 1838, with symbols of Maryland and the union of the thirteen colonies.
moments.notice: Washington’s figure depicts his resignation as commander-in-chief, rather than a battlefield command.

moments.title: Charles Village
moments.text: Charles Village began as Peabody Heights, a development launched with a fifty-acre land purchase in 1869. Builders supplied the house exteriors and left interiors to be fitted to buyers’ specifications. The name Charles Village was coined in the 1970s, drawing together a larger, varied area under the name of its main north-south street. Much of its housing consists of two- and three-story rowhouses built in the early twentieth century. St. Paul Street serves as the neighborhood’s main commercial street. Brick and stone rowhouses, including homes dating from the 1890s, are part of the neighborhood’s housing.

moments.title: Homewood Museum
moments.text: Homewood’s red brick and white marble became a model for Johns Hopkins University’s campus design. The estate was offered in 1800 as a wedding gift from Charles Carroll of Carrollton to his son, Charles Carroll Jr. The son began building the house in 1801 and had mostly finished it by 1808. Its $40,000 cost was four times the budget. The house later served as a school, a faculty club and university offices before opening as a museum in 1987. Maryland’s tourism office describes museum tours that examine the connected lives of the house’s free and enslaved inhabitants.
moments.notice: A four-column portico dominates the house’s main facade.
